summary.title: MTTR is more important than MTBF (for most types of F)
summary.one_liner: Recovering quickly from failure (low mean time to repair) usually matters more than failing less often (high mean time between failures), except for failures that should never happen, such as data loss.
takeaways: MTTR (mean time to repair) is argued to be more important than MTBF (mean time between failures) for most types of failure.
Some failures, such as accidental data loss, should never happen, so the MTTR argument has exceptions.
Investing in response to failure can be as valuable as trying to prevent it, since failure will happen.
Dark launches, percentage-based rollouts and feature flags are cited as practices that support designing for fast recovery.
The Jeep vs Rolls Royce comparison illustrates designing for easy repair rather than for avoiding breakdowns.
summary.summary: This is a short blog post by John Allspaw, adapted from a QCon SF talk on development and operations cooperation at Etsy and Flickr. He argues that recovering quickly from failure matters more than preventing failures, with the caveat that some failures should never happen. He uses Artur Bergman's Jeep versus Rolls Royce analogy to show designing for easy repair instead of long mean time between failures. He closes by linking deployment practices such as dark launching, percentage-based rollouts and feature flags as support for this approach.
